summary: Describes the xcap-diff SIP event package, which lets clients receive notifications when XCAP resources change. The initial sync and later updates use the XCAP diff format. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: You sign up to get a message whenever your shared documents change, instead of checking them over and over.

questions: what is the xcap-diff event package
how to subscribe to xcap changes
subtitle: A SIP event package that tells clients when XCAP documents change, so they do not have to keep polling.

tldr.problem: XCAP lets several clients edit the same XML document but gives no effective way, beyond polling, to keep a client's copy in step with the server.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends a SIP SUBSCRIBE for the "xcap-diff" event with a list of XCAP URLs, and the notifier answers with NOTIFY requests that carry XCAP diff documents, in one of three change-reporting modes chosen with the diff-processing parameter.
tldr.outcome: Clients get an initial synchronization and then updates, either as plain change events or as XML patches, which can greatly reduce the number of notifications and transmissions. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Notification rate
facts.value: Not more than once every five seconds (SHOULD)

today: RFC 5875 is a Proposed Standard from May 2010. The metadata for this RFC lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It relies on the diff format in RFC 5874.

sections.title: Replacing Polling with Subscriptions
sections.content:
The SIP events framework (RFC 3265) defines subscriptions and notifications for the Session Initiation Protocol (RFC 3261). XCAP (RFC 4825) lets clients read, write and modify XML data on a server. When several authorized users or devices edit the same document, XCAP offers nothing beyond polling to keep their copies synchronized.

This RFC defines the xcap-diff event package. Together with the SIP event framework and the XCAP diff format (RFC 5874), it lets a user subscribe to changes in XML documents and receive a notification whenever one changes.

It enables three basic features:

  • Subscribing to a list of document URLs in a collection, so the subscriber can compare the URLs and strong ETags with its local copies and synchronize.
  • Signalling a change in one of three ways: event type only (the subscriber then uses HTTP to fetch the document), minimal-size XML patches, or verbose patches that show the full version history.
  • Subscribing to specific elements or attributes (XCAP components) and receiving their existing contents, including a notification when a component is later created or removed.
sections.eli5: You tell a messenger which pages in the shared notebook you care about. The messenger tells you when they change, and you choose how much detail you want.

sections.title: Overview and Basic Rules
sections.content:
To subscribe, the client puts a URI list in the SUBSCRIBE body. Each URL MUST be an HTTP URL that identifies a collection, an XCAP document or an XCAP component. Collection URLs MUST end in a forward slash, and a collection selection includes all documents in that collection and, recursively, in its sub-collections. A component URL is the document URL plus an XCAP Node Selector. Clients MUST NOT subscribe to namespaces.

The notifier MUST support XCAP component subscriptions. It sends the first notification in response to the subscription, and that notification MUST contain the URLs of the documents and component contents in the subscription. Later notifications MAY contain patches.

The event package name is xcap-diff and appears in the Event header field of SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY. Subscriptions last 3600 seconds by default, and the subscriber MAY ask for another time with the Expires header field. Notifiers SHOULD NOT send notifications for one subscription more often than once every five seconds. State agents play no role in this package, and only a single dialog may result from an initial SUBSCRIBE, so forked responses are handled as RFC 3265 describes for non-allowed forking.
sections.eli5: You hand over a list of the pages you want to watch. A first message tells you what exists right now, and later messages tell you about changes, but not too often.

sections.title: The diff-processing Parameter
sections.content:
The optional diff-processing parameter of the Event header field is the subscriber's hint about how change notifications for documents should be shown. It has three values:

  • no-patching: the notification names the document and the event type (creation, modification or removal) and does not necessarily give the full ETag history. Notifiers MUST support it as the interoperability baseline.
  • xcap-patching: the notifier includes all updated component contents and ETag changes made by XCAP clients, so the subscriber sees the full ETag change history.
  • aggregate: the notifier MAY combine several component updates into a single <document> element. How much to aggregate is a local decision.

Without the parameter the notifier MUST default to no-patching. The notifier SHOULD use the requested mode if it understands it, and it SHOULD support xcap-patching and aggregate too, because they can greatly reduce the number of notifications. The subscriber MAY change the parameter on re-subscription. The parameter has no effect on component subscriptions.

The RFC's example: a document has versions a, b and c with ETags 1, 2 and 3. In xcap-patching mode the notifier reports a to b (ETags 1 and 2) and then b to c (ETags 2 and 3). In aggregate mode it reports a single change from a to c (ETags 1 and 3).
sections.eli5: You pick how chatty the messenger should be: just "page 5 changed", a full list of every edit, or one short summary of all edits together.

sections.title: SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY Bodies
sections.content:
The SUBSCRIBE body is a resource list document (RFC 4826) in a simple flat form: the uri attribute of each <entry> holds one XCAP request URI. Hierarchical lists and <entry-ref> MUST NOT be used. A later SUBSCRIBE, such as a refresh, MAY change the list, and the notifier MUST then use the new one. Relative URIs are allowed because the XCAP server is usually co-located with the SIP notifier, which therefore MUST know how to resolve them against the XCAP root.

An Accept header field is optional. If it is absent, the default is application/xcap-diff+xml, and if it is present it MUST include that type. A SUBSCRIBE MAY carry a Suppress-If-Match header field (RFC 5839) for conditional subscriptions. Unknown elements or attributes in the body MUST be ignored.

NOTIFY bodies contain an XCAP diff document. The sel values MUST be octet-by-octet equal to the matching uri values in the subscription, except for collection selections. When component subscriptions use namespace prefixes, the notifier MUST resolve them as RFC 4825 describes.
sections.eli5: Your list of pages goes in the sign-up form, and the messenger's updates come back in the standard note format from the companion document.

sections.title: How the Notifier Behaves
sections.content:
On the initial subscription, or when a refresh changes the list, the notifier MUST resolve the requested resources and the subscriber's privileges. A resource the user may not read MUST NOT appear in the diff. A component that cannot be found is not an error: the request stays pending until the resource is created or access is granted. A subscribed collection works the same way, so a newly created document is signalled in the next NOTIFY.

The first NOTIFY lists the existing, readable documents and typically the existing components. After that, the notifier picks a mode. It MAY use the requested mode or fall back to a simpler one, but MUST NOT use a more complex one. From simplest to most complex the order is no-patching, xcap-patching, aggregate. In every mode chronological order MUST be preserved in the XML document order.

Aggregation saves the most bandwidth but has a cost: initial synchronization of rapidly changing resources might fail because the full version history is not included. The notifier may also be unable to produce patches in corner cases such as a change to the XML prolog, and it MAY temporarily send only URI references, for example when the body would be impractically large.

Removals must be reported consistently: after reporting a component, the notifier MUST report its removal by setting exist to false on the element or attribute, and for fast-changing resources it MUST signal only the latest state. A notifier MAY drop element content if the body would be too large, leaving an empty <element>.

Re-subscriptions normally cause the full state to be resent, unless the subscriber uses a conditional subscription with Suppress-If-Match and the stored state matches. NOTIFY delivery must be reliable. The notifier MUST NOT send a new NOTIFY on a dialog until a 200 response was received for the last one, and if a NOTIFY fails due to a timeout it MUST remove the subscription.
sections.eli5: The messenger only tells you about pages you may read, keeps the news in the right order, waits for you to say "got it" before sending the next message, and stops if you stop answering.

sections.title: How the Subscriber Stays in Sync
sections.content:
The first NOTIFY usually has URLs and strong ETags. If the subscriber has no matching cached version, it typically does an HTTP GET. While it waits, patches may arrive for a rapidly changing document. The subscriber then walks the chain of changes, finds the change whose previous ETag equals the one it fetched, skips earlier changes and applies all later patches. If the fetched version is newer than anything in the notifications, it may find no match, and it can re-fetch, wait for later notifications or refresh the subscription and repeat until it is fully synchronized.

Aggregation can hide the ETag the subscriber fetched. To avoid that, the subscriber MAY start in xcap-patching mode and switch to aggregate after the initial sync, and it can switch back at any time. If some resources are served in xcap-patching and others in aggregate after a full sync, it SHOULD refresh to aggregate.

The notifier MAY temporarily fall back to no-patching at any time, so the subscriber is always responsible for taking the right action, and as a last resort it MAY set the parameter to no-patching itself. If a patch cannot be applied, the subscriber SHOULD refresh the subscription with no-patching and SHOULD NOT reply with a non-200 response, because the notifier cannot make corrections. On an unconditional re-subscription the subscriber MUST mark all previous state as stale, while after a successful conditional one it MUST keep the current state unless the URI list changed.
sections.eli5: If your photocopy does not match the news, you find where the news lines up with your copy, skip the old edits and apply the rest. If that fails, ask for plain "page changed" notices and fetch the page again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All the security considerations of RFC 3265 apply. Because configuration data can be sensitive, client and server need to authenticate each other. Notifiers MUST authenticate subscribers with the normal SIP mechanisms, for example Digest as in Section 22 of RFC 3261, and MUST map authenticated SIP identities unambiguously to XCAP User Identifiers (XUIs). Notifiers MUST also obey XCAP authorization, which in practice means the read privilege rules, and the security considerations of XCAP apply.

Denial of service against notifiers gets special mention. Intensive processing can come from subscriptions to a long list of URIs, pending subscriptions to documents or components that do not exist, and diff-generation algorithms that push bandwidth optimization to extremes. The transport MUST ensure integrity and SHOULD ensure confidentiality. S/MIME SHOULD be used end to end, and if not available, TLS between elements is RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: The messenger checks who you are before telling you anything, and only shares pages you are allowed to read. Asking about a huge pile of pages could tire the messenger out.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA added one entry to the SIP Event Types Namespace registry: package name xcap-diff, type package, contact IETF Real-time Applications (rai@ietf.org), reference RFC 5875.
sections.eli5: The new event gets its name written in the official list of SIP events.

viz.caption: THE THREE diff-processing VALUES, SIMPLEST TO MOST COMPLEX

items.label: Event type only
items.desc: Names the document and event type; subscriber fetches by HTTP. Default, and every notifier MUST support it.

items.label: Full version history
items.desc: Each change is reported with its previous and new ETag.

items.label: Combined changes
items.desc: Several updates may be merged into one change from the first to the last ETag.

viz.caption: EXAMPLE SUBSCRIBE HEADERS AND BODY (FROM THE RFC, ABBREVIATED)

data.title: Subscription with a URI list
data.code:
SUBSCRIBE sip:tests@xcap.example.com SIP/2.0
...
Accept: application/xcap-diff+xml
Event: xcap-diff; diff-processing=aggregate
Content-Type: application/resource-lists+xml
Expires: 4200

<resource-lists xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:resource-lists">
 <list>
  <entry uri="resource-lists/users/sip:joe@example.com/index"/>
  <entry uri="pidf-manipulation/"/>
 </list>
</resource-lists>
